slides.label: Title
slides.notes: Open by framing angle measure as a test for what the model is allowed to preserve. The chapter is not merely about assigning degrees to a drawing; it asks which measurements come from directions, which depend on the chosen line system, and which survive a conformal change of metric.

slides.label: Route
slides.notes: Use the route as a contract for the lecture. Each topic starts with a primitive object, translates it into a measurable predicate, and then checks where that predicate is stable or fragile. Keep returning to the three labels metric, model-dependent, and conformal so students classify each result.

slides.label: Direction Formula
slides.notes: Stress that the point O is not measured by itself; the data are the two outgoing directions. Normalizing rays removes their lengths, while the dot and determinant together locate the angle without ambiguity. The displayed formulas are computational versions of the protractor idea.

slides.label: Notebook Direction Artifact
slides.notes: Read the artifact as an inspection target. The ray lengths are arbitrary, but the normalized directions and the marked arc determine the reported angle. Ask students what would change if the same rays were translated, scaled, or reflected, and separate measurement from the drawing.

slides.label: Perpendicularity And Congruence
slides.notes: Present perpendicularity as a special angle condition rather than as a picture of a cross. Use the congruence graphic to connect synthetic language with computation: a rigid move changes coordinates but should not alter side lengths or angle measures, so the invariant inventory matters more than the screen picture.

slides.label: Molton Warning
slides.notes: Slow down on the Molton warning because it is the chapter's antidote to overconfident Euclidean intuition. The model keeps a plane-like set of points but changes what some lines mean. Once the carrier lines bend, ordinary slope pictures no longer certify angle facts.

slides.label: Molton Local Test
slides.notes: Explain the diagram as a rule book, not as a defect in drawing. On one side of the vertical divider the familiar line direction is kept; on the other side positive slopes are reinterpreted. Angle statements must therefore name the model before they can be measured.

slides.label: Poincare Conformality
slides.notes: For the Poincare disk, emphasize the contrast between distance and angle. Hyperbolic distances are distorted by the disk model, but angles are measured by Euclidean tangent directions at intersections of geodesics. That conformal feature lets local angle reasoning look familiar inside a non-Euclidean metric.

slides.label: Poincare Artifact
slides.notes: Use the artifact to make tangent direction concrete. The boundary circle is not decoration; Poincare geodesics meet it orthogonally, and the angle at an interior crossing is read from their tangent lines. Students should distinguish the circular arc itself from its tangent direction at the point.

slides.label: Model Comparison
slides.notes: Treat the table as a classification device. Euclidean diagrams, Molton diagrams, and Poincare disk diagrams can look deceptively similar on a slide, so students should ask what counts as a line, what counts as a direction, and which transformations preserve the chosen measure.

slides.label: Worked Numeric Check
slides.notes: Work the numeric example slowly, because it turns a formal angle definition into an audit trail. The coordinates produce vectors, the vectors produce a dot product and a determinant, and those two numbers feed atan2 to give the same acute-looking angle without relying on a protractor.

slides.label: Recap
slides.notes: Close by asking students to carry the three tests into later chapters. When congruence, parallelism, and hyperbolic constructions appear, the same question returns: is the statement about metric size, about the model's primitive lines, or about angle data preserved by a conformal map?
